results.summary: This project implements a ring oscillator with a 64-bit counter to test a power switching FET. The counter increments based on oscillations from the ring oscillator and can be reset or stopped via dedicated input pins. The counter's value can be shifted using input pins, and the lower 8 bits of the counter are output. Silicon testing confirmed the design is working, with measurements indicating the ring oscillator operates at approximately 504 MHz.

This project consists of 128 daisy-chained D flip-flops, intended for testing or demonstration purposes. The design is implemented using Wokwi, suggesting it is primarily a simulation-based project. Testing and usage require specific external hardware called 'encabultors' connected to the input and output. The exact functionality and purpose are not fully detailed in the provided documentation.

This project displays a bouncing ball on a 640x480 VGA-style display, controlled via SPI commands. The design includes a VGA timing generator, SPI receiver, command decoder, and a physics engine. Users can send commands over SPI to set the ball's position and velocity, with the ball updating every six frames and rebounding off screen edges. The design is intended for a TinyVGA PMOD connection and has a testbench for verification.

This is an 8-bit processor designed to communicate with external devices via SPI and animate a seven-segment display. It requires an external driver, such as an FPGA, to load programs and control execution. Users can view processor register contents or observe animations on the display after assembling and loading programs. The design supports animating the seven-segment display and offers options to view instruction or data memory contents.

This project is a demoscene-style VGA generator that produces a 640x480 @ 60Hz video signal without frame buffers or external memory. It features a procedurally generated animated background and a central logo inspired by the Tiny Tapeout mark. The design uses reduced-resolution coordinates for a retro visual style and can be controlled via input pins to invert colors or freeze the logo. A VGA PMOD is required for video output.

This project is a 4-bit high-security password system implemented using logic gates, designed to grant access for a correct code and trigger a persistent alarm for an incorrect code. It utilizes an SR latch to maintain the alarm state, requiring a manual reset. The system is tested by configuring inputs via a DIP switch and observing the output LEDs and buzzer. The documentation lists several external hardware components used in its simulation.

This project implements a 1D Kalman Filter for fusing accelerometer and gyroscope data from an MPU-6500 sensor, calculating Roll and Pitch angles. It includes an SPI master to interface with the sensor, a CORDIC core for angle estimation, and a UART transmitter to output the results. The design is intended to be tested on hardware using an FPGA ASIC simulator breakout with an MPU-6500 sensor and an FT232 serial probe. The output angles are transmitted as a binary stream at 9600 baud.

This is a silicon implementation of Conway's Game of Life played on an 8x32 grid, designed to output to a MAX7219 LED Matrix. The rules of the Game of Life are implemented in hardware, and the grid state can be displayed directly or sent to an LED matrix. The project supports both a demo mode with pre-defined patterns and a manual mode for loading custom initial grids. Silicon testing confirmed it works on an LED matrix, though a minor bug causes a delay before animations start.

This project implements an 8-bit Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR) circuit using Verilog. The LFSR is a type of pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) commonly used in digital systems for various applications like testing and generating pseudorandom sequences. The design has 8 output pins, but all input pins are marked as unused, indicating it operates as a standalone sequential block. Further details on its specific application or testing methodology are not provided.

This project, named DigOTA, functions as a digital Operational Transconductance Amplifier (OTA). It requires a 50kHz clock signal and takes two inputs, producing three outputs. The documentation states that the output current is proportional to the number of pulses in the output stages. The design is implemented in Wokwi, suggesting it is primarily intended for simulation and educational purposes.
